This paper introduces the TVP-AR(p) model, a novel extension of the classical Poisson autoregressive model designed to capture time-varying autocorrelation within count data. We demonstrate that the likelihood function for the TVP-AR(p) model can be expressed as a product involving the L\'evy score process of a non-negative stationary process governed by a first-order smooth transition process. To estimate the model's parameters, we propose a simulation-based approach that combines importance sampling with data augmentation. The effectiveness of the TVP-AR(p) model in identifying structural breaks in count data is validated through simulations, while its utility in detecting business cycle turning points in firm-level investment decisions is illustrated using real-world data. Additionally, the application of the TVP-AR(p) model to monitor structural changes in crime trends is explored. As a temporal variation model, TVP-AR(p) offers significant advantages for identifying structural breaks and detecting shifts in count data; its utility in real-time anomaly detection is also highlighted. Finally, a future direction for developing a time-series forecasting model based on TVP-AR(p) to support real-time decision-making is discussed. Keywords: Count data, simulation-based estimation, structural break detection, anoma.

While previous work by the authors has examined the limitations of using human comments as gold standards for assessing automated image description systems, this approach has not yet established a specific methodology for integrating those comments during evaluation. This paper does not fill that gap; instead, we explore alternative strategies for leveraging human feedback when measuring the quality of match between automatic and manual image descriptions. Specifically, we introduce a method to quantify the distance between an automated description and a image using the corresponding human reference, thereby creating a direct, metric-based evaluation framework that utilizes but does not depend on the actual text of the human annotation. This study presents a self-consistent model of baryon and meson production that extends beyond the capabilities of current state-of-the-art predictions. Utilizing an imaginary-time formalism, we derive a simple, universal scaling solution for both species without relying on the assumption of identical scaling behaviors between them. Crucially, this approach requires only one baryon-to-meson ratio at a specific scale to determine all other ratios, eliminating the need to fix the absolute scale itself. Consequently, every ratio becomes a universal function of the invariant mass scale. Once all meson and baryon spectra are determined by this ratio and the universal scaling functions, the absolute yields are fixed solely by the total energy density. We anticipate that this framework will prove valuable for analyzing particle spectra across various collision systems and centers of mass energy. Furthermore, it offers the unique capability to test the universality of the universal functions themselves. Specifically, we can examine whether the ratio of every meson spectrum to the pion spectrum (and similarly for other baryons) follows a universal scaling behavior when viewed as a function of invariant mass, across different collision systems and baryon species. The same verification process applies to the scaling functions governing the relative spectra of different baryons. As an initial step, we focus on proton predictions for proton-proton collisions, where the calculated yields align reasonably well with measured data. This paper examines a point-to-point integrated data and power delivery system, modeled as a single-link data channel supplemented by multiple access points, each providing power to a specific segment of the data channel. We evaluate two potential solutions: an optimal non-linear solution utilizing multi-carrier modulation with dedicated power transmission on a separate carrier, and a near-optimal linear solution based on multi-carrier modulation with superposition for both data and power. The study involves developing a non-linear scheduling algorithm for the optimal approach and a multi-step algorithm for the linear approach. Additionally, we create a comprehensive characterization framework to identify the ideal performance gap between these methods and other potential solutions. The frameworks and algorithms are validated through simulations and field trials. Findings indicate that the optimal non-linear solution and the proposed multi-carrier linear solution achieve significant improvements over current state-of-the-art approaches—specifically time-division multiple access and a specialized multi-carrier method with fixed weighting for the power signal. These gains vary between 17% and 27% of the total data rate. Moreover, the non-linear and multi-carrier linear solutions enable the system to meet specified data rate requirements with an order of magnitude lower noise figure than the state-of-the-art solution. Lastly, for the non-linear and multi-carrier linear solutions, prioritizing data segments with higher rates per hertz (as determined by the data-only channel state) yields the greatest overall data rate increases. These results support the conclusion that the choice of modulation strategy for the power signal and the associated scheduling algorithm can produce substantial performance gains. The proposed non-linear and multi-carrier linear solutions with their respective algorithms offer a viable pathway for integrating data and power without requiring infrastructure upgrades or specialized DC-to-AC conversion units at individual segments. This makes the approach particularly well-suited for municipal wide-area data and power networks. This study employs a structured linearized approach to simulate the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and acoustic waves. Using this model, researchers investigated whether the fire would oscillate when exposed to plane acoustic waves at various frequencies and amplitudes. Linear stability analysis revealed a dominant global oscillation mode at 171 Hz, driven by the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability within the turbulent jet. When the incident acoustic wave amplitude remained low, the resulting oscillations were linear; however, higher amplitudes triggered non-linear behaviors, including the emergence of secondary modes and limit cycle oscillations. These findings align well with recent experimental results, confirming the model's validity. Ultimately, this linearized framework serves as an effective tool for assessing how fires respond to acoustic excitations without requiring costly and complex experiments. Furthermore, the model can be adapted to explore the impact of flame-stabilizing coflowing jets on oscillations and to analyze the effects of geometric modifications on these dynamics. Nonlocal gravity models serve as effective frameworks for addressing anomalies in orbital accelerations within the Solar System and other astrophysical systems, without requiring extra mass components or nonlocal modifications to gravitational laws. These approaches rely on constitutive relations that link nonlocal gravitational effects to the nonlocal history of matter distributions. Recently, a formalism was developed to integrate these constitutive relations into the field-theoretic BiGravitation model, successfully accounting for acceleration anomalies via nonlocal terms. However, BiGravitation remains a specific implementation, and its capabilities are constrained by the feasibility of solving its nonlocal field equations. This paper introduces a more general approach: embedding these relations into the Einstein field equations to create a fully nonlocal theory. We demonstrate that, for diagonal constitutive matrices, these equations can be efficiently resolved nonlocally using an essential tensor defined as the product of the nonlocal acceleration between two points and the unit direction tensor. Similarly, between any pair of points, one can define a nonlocal curvature tensor analogously to the Riemann tensor, and an associated Einstein tensor. We further show that the nonlocal Einstein tensor and the local Einstein tensor do not share the same trace, necessitating a new constitutive relation for a nonlocal cosmological constant term. Finally, we establish a constitutive relationship between the nonlocal Riemann tensor and the Rankin tensor, which describes nonlocal tidal forces.

This presentation reports on selected LHC experiments involving large and small systems. While the discussion covers a range of topics, the primary focus will be on recent findings related to collective phenomena in p-p and ion-pion collisions. It will also address the challenges and opportunities presented by analyzing tiny systems with low multiplicity events. Additionally, the talk will highlight results from a unique study of 109 Iron-Iron collisions, which dates back to the year 1936. The variable luminosity of X-ray binaries near the Galactic Centre, particularly those with low mass functions, is likely regulated by accretion instabilities triggered when mass accretion rates exceed a specific threshold. While this critical rate is definitively known for neutron star binaries with transient behaviors, it remains uncertain for those without variable or transient activities. Given that the Galactic Centre's dormant binaries have not exhibited outbursts over the past two decades, their accretion rates in the last twenty years have likely remained below this critical value. By analyzing the luminosity intervals of transients in the past two decades for nine neutron star binaries with low mass functions at the Galactic Centre, we established a linear relationship between these intervals and the stars' peak luminosity during outbursts. Using the linearity slope, the duration of transients in the past two decades for at least one binary with a known critical accretion rate, and the long-term average accretion rate of a binary with varying luminosity, we calculated the critical mass accretion rate at $3.4(-1.0,+2.0)\times10{-}9$ times the solar mass per year. Correspondingly, the critical luminosity was determined to be $0.016(-0.005,+0.008)$ times solar luminosity. These calculations assume that the mass function of the binary with variable transients at the Galactic Centre fluctuates minimally between variations spanning two decades. Furthermore, we posit that transients observed in the past two decades for this binary result from TONNE 1-type instabilities, whereas longer-duration variations arise from QTONNE 1-type instabilities. Finally, we discuss these findings in relation to recent observations of a transient in the IGR J17591$-$3107 binary after a two-decade lapse.

Bipartite graphs represent a specific type of graph where vertices can be split into two independent sets. This paper examines the problem of partitioning the vertex set of a simple, connected, weighted, bipartite graph $G$ into two connected, independent subsets $A$ and $B$, such that the weighted edge between them is minimized. This optimization task is known as the weighted bipartite cut problem and is applicable in scenarios like optimizing two-school systems or dividing voters into two election districts. Currently, this problem is solved using a meet-in-the-middle approach combined with a recently developed edge-nudging algorithm. Our meta-heuristic also employs the meet-in-the-middle strategy but replaces the edge-nudging algorithm with a novel meta-heuristic called full-mode simulated annealing. Additionally, we introduce a fresh meet-in-the-middle algorithm that operates without either the edge-nudging or full-mode simulated annealing methods. Experimental results indicate that this latest algorithm outperforms all previous approaches. These findings suggest that the full graph structure is not necessary for such optimization problems; instead, a meta-heuristic focusing primarily on the vertex set between two parts is sufficient. This insight opens new directions for researching meta-heuristics in other combinatorial optimization problems. Specifically, we developed the first meeting-treework and refined full-mode simulated annealing algorithms for a challenge involving covering red and blue points in the plane with a minimum number of triangles. Our experiments demonstrate that both algorithms surpass existing meta-heuristics, solving the problem significantly faster than prior methods, including a recent exhaustive search. These results confirm that the new approaches effectively handle large-scale instances of this difficult problem, which has long resisted solutions from traditional techniques like genetic algorithms or tabu search. Furthermore, these methods have been applied to two real-world scenarios: optimally assigning students to two high schools in New Caledonia and distributing voters into two districts for New Zealand's upcoming general election. Finally, we plan to extend this work by developing a bi-criteria optimization algorithm that minimizes both the number of weighted edges between parts and the absolute difference in vertex counts (representing party balance) between the two sets.

This paper introduces a multi-scale tactical game designed to evaluate how conventional networks of robots with limited computational and communication capabilities collaborate. The proposed game model considers three distinct enemy actions: direct attacks on individual robots, strikes targeting their communication links, and assaults on their backend infrastructure. A real-time multi-agent planning algorithm based on a modified means-end analysis (MEA) approach is developed to navigate this environment. Additionally, the results indicate that prioritizing critical goals and employing a prioritized MEA algorithm over utility maximization effectively enhances collaborative multi-agent performance in the face of communication loss and infrastructure damage. We present ATOMIC, an atlas of machine-commonsense knowledge designed to support the generation of if-then inference rules. This system connects entities with events or situations via predicates, followed by a description of an outcome, action, or recommendation in natural language. To ensure these events and related predicates are modelled by symbolic solvers amenable to if-then inference, ATOMIC employs a symbolic solver to verify events constructed by a language model. Consequently, only events successfully verified are added to the atlas. Demonstrating the feasibility of such an end-to-end approach, we introduce a dataset of if-then inference pairs derived from ATOMIC itself. Although focusing on a narrow format, this data serves to highlight gaps in the commonsense knowledge supplied by the underlying solver and language model, offering a valuable resource for evaluating both. Finally, we outline several potential applications for the if-then inference dataset and the ATOMIC system itself. At a minimum, ATOMIC serves as a valuable benchmark for evaluating agents on conditional reasoning tasks in natural language, whether through if-then pairs or separate premise and hypothesis sentences. Regarding the dataset, we do not claim it constitutes a true solution, as creating such a dataset remains an open challenge. Furthermore, generating an atlas like ATOMIC to enable solving if-then pairs is a specific strategy for addressing this problem, potentially acting as a component within a broader pipeline that handles more complex conditionals, such as open-ended counterfactuals. Ultimately, the concept of an atlas encompassing both events and their corresponding if-then rules is merely one possible solution to this difficult problem, which requires further research to fully resolve. Our dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/atomic-commonsense/conditional-reasoning. Additionally, the ATOMIC system itself is available as a separate open-source project at https://github.com/atomic-commonsense/atomic.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\beta(G)$, represents the dimension of an optimal embedding for $G$ into a path that preserves distances as much as possible. In this work, we examine the extended definition of metric dimension associated with a weighted geodesic metric. Specifically, we define the $\kappa$-metric dimension, which corresponds to the dimension required for embedding $G$ into a path while restricting the distorted distance between any pair of vertices to exceed the original geodesic distance by no more than $\kappa$. We introduce the concept of $\kappa$-metric dimension and analyze the properties of the function $\beta_\kappa(G)$. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for the $\beta_\kappa(C_n)$ of a cycle and determine the exact value for paths and trees. Additionally, for a graph $G$ with diameter $d(G)$, we establish that $\beta_{d(G)}(G) = |V(G)| - 1$. Our findings regarding the $\kappa$-metric dimension of cycles reveal significant insights into the structure of cycles themselves. Mathematical models of disease transmission were initially created during the 1920/1921 outbreak of Spanish influenza and subsequently refined over the last century to investigate theoretical concerns and support practical decisions during various epidemics. In the current global pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, there is a risk that models are deployed too hastily to guide immediate actions without sufficient consideration of their underlying assumptions, structural limitations, and uncertainties. While the specific form of a model for this epidemic has evolved rapidly in response to new data and policy shifts, several core components have remained consistent: an epidemiological compartmental structure to integrate available information; a geographic dimension to address varying local interventions; and an temporal element adapted to the pace of data collection and decision-making. Although no single canonical structure has emerged, a typical framework comprises three interrelated elements: a compartmental design (often incorporating mutation and viral evolution), a statistical component for parameter estimation and forecasting, and a theoretical segment for analyzing dynamical properties like the basic reproduction number $R_0$ and its generalizations (e.g., time-dependent $R_t$). This article examines these three components in the context of the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 response, offering recommendations for future research directions. Additionally, we provide references to recent studies aligning with these three areas, acknowledging that the field is rapidly expanding beyond the examples selected here due to constraints in scope. Ultimately, this paper does not advocate for one specific model structure over another; rather, it highlights the essential elements required for any viable model and emphasizes the need for concurrent research into their epidemiological, statistical, and theoretical aspects. Such a holistic approach ensures models are fit for purpose, grounded in sound epidemiological theory, capable of handling data through appropriate statistical methods, and able of addressing key questions regarding system dynamics. Only by meeting these criteria can the scientific community draw reliable conclusions about the epidemic's dynamics and the efficacy of control measures, while policymakers can be assured that the recommended actions are supported by robust epidemiological evidence. Regarding the article's title, the use of "outbreaks" rather than "epidemics" intentionally distingu between small-scale events requiring localized interventions and large-scale widespread events, as the research community has already experienced both phases with SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and now with SARS-CoV-2.

This study examines the fractional changes in observable shadows and their associated thermodynamics for both static and rotating non-linear charged AdS black holes. The analysis reveals that, when ordered by shadow size, the shadow of a non-linear charged AdS black hole is larger than that of a non-neutral non-linear AdS black hole, which in turn is larger than the shadow of a unit charged non-linear AdS black hole. These findings indicate that the shadow radius and the dimensionless charge parameter are inversely related, while the shadow radius is directly related to the other thermodynamic variables. These results suggest that black hole shadows serve as a valuable tool for investigating the thermodynamic properties of non-linear charged AdS black holes. The related visualizations and experimental setups are discussed in conjunction with these results.

This study investigates the regular intervals observed in the pulsating crackling sound generated when pulling an adhesive tape through its peeled region to separate it from a surface. These intervals suggest periodicity in the sound production mechanism. Using a model where an unstable snapping mechanism alternates with a build-up phase, we demonstrate that this periodicity arises from a "concealed" mechanical instability occurring within the already-snapped segment. While this secondary instability has negligible impact on the overall motion of the tape, it significantly influences the timing of the sound emissions. To validate this theoretical framework, we collected data from tape samples with varying material and geometric properties, as well as from commercially available "masking" and "painter"s tapes with known characteristics. Additional experiments conducted on an eraser and an adhesive note were also analyzed to further support the model. Ultimately, this simple yet effective model may offer insights into the periodic sound patterns produced by other systems undergoing shear-induced failure. Situational linear bandits model decision-making in complex environments where agents operate as if embedded in a specific situation, drawing on a feature vector to represent that situation without explicitly defining it. These agents function within a framework where the environment is distributed, potentially unknown, and potentially without a underlying structure.
